title: In the Matter of Baby M
lead: A paid promise to surrender a child proved unenforceable, but the child’s custody still required an independent best-interests decision between her natural parents.

actors.name: William and Elizabeth Stern
actors.role: Intended father and prospective adoptive mother

proceedings: Trial court enforced the contract, terminated maternal rights, awarded William custody, and allowed Elizabeth’s adoption.
New Jersey Supreme Court reversed termination and adoption, affirmed William’s custody, and remanded visitation to a different judge.
limits: The ruling concerns the 1988 statutes and this paid irrevocable agreement, not present surrogacy law. It did not find either natural parent unfit, award custody as punishment, or order an immediate unrestricted visitation schedule.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The parties arrange insemination and paid surrender
sections.cue: The written terms allocate parental rights and pregnancy control
paragraphs: William Stern wanted a biological child; Elizabeth feared pregnancy might worsen possible multiple sclerosis. Her anxiety was genuine, although medical evidence indicated relatively small pregnancy risk. Through the Infertility Center of New York, William arranged for Mary Beth Whitehead to conceive with his sperm, carry the child, surrender custody, and cooperate in terminating her parental rights for Elizabeth’s adoption. Richard Whitehead agreed to relinquish any rights and rebut presumed paternity. Elizabeth was not a contracting party.

William promised Mary Beth $10,000 on delivery and completion of her obligations and the center $7,500 separately. The court regarded initial motives as sincere: a family for the Sterns, and for Mary Beth both helping an infertile couple and obtaining money for her own family.

The document assigned pregnancy risks including death to the Whiteheads, specified time-limited medical payments, required examinations and compliance with instructions, and promised Elizabeth custody if William died. A fetal-abnormality clause required abortion on his demand, with refusal ending his contractual duties apart from statutory paternity obligations; undetected abnormalities remained his responsibility. Voluntary-execution language and severability also appeared. These were contractual demands, not judicial approvals of each provision.

sections.title: Surrender is followed by distress and refusal to return the child
sections.cue: Enforcement proceedings produce a contested temporary custody
paragraphs: The child was born March 27, 1986. Mary Beth surrendered her March 30, became severely distressed, and requested a week with her. Concerned by her despair, the Sterns agreed. She then refused return. William sued and obtained an ex parte transfer order. Richard escaped through a window with the baby, and the Whiteheads fled among numerous Florida lodgings. Recorded calls included threats of suicide, killing the child, and falsely accusing William of abusing another daughter.

Florida authorities eventually enforced return to the Sterns. The trial court maintained temporary custody and limited Mary Beth’s visits. After a thirty-two-day trial, it upheld the agreement, terminated her rights, awarded William sole custody, and allowed Elizabeth to adopt. It treated best interests as a prerequisite to specifically enforcing a valid bargain.

Mary Beth appealed, challenging legality and constitutionality and seeking custody partly to deter surrogacy. The Sterns defended the contract and reproductive privacy. The guardian advocated the child’s interests without taking a contract-validity position. The Supreme Court granted direct certification.

sections.title: Existing adoption protections invalidate the bargain
sections.cue: Contractual consent cannot substitute for statutory termination
paragraphs: Chief Justice Wilentz’s unanimous opinion identified three independent statutory conflicts. First, adoption law prohibited payment connected with placement apart from approved-agency fees and specified medical expenses. Calling $10,000 service compensation and leaving Elizabeth off the agreement did not change payment conditioned on surrender and termination; fetal death yielded markedly less or none despite services. The court described possible criminal illegality without convicting anyone.

Second, outside qualifying formal agency surrender, termination required stringent abandonment, serious-neglect, or comparable grounds, not a better alternative home. Neither stepparent adoption nor Parentage Act best-interests language removed that protection. Mary Beth had not abandoned the child; the trial court had not found her unfit and called her a good mother to her older children. Fighting to retain this child did not show forsaking her. Without lawful termination, Elizabeth’s adoption failed.

Third, the contract made surrender irrevocable before conception, bypassing prescribed post-birth agency procedures, acknowledgment, and counseling. Private consent could be withdrawn and did not alone establish termination grounds. These central promises rendered the whole bargain unenforceable despite severability language.

sections.title: Policy and constitutional arguments do not rescue enforcement
sections.cue: The court reserves broader constitutional questions
paragraphs: The agreement fixed custody and permanent separation before assessing the child’s interests, prospective custodians, or maternal wishes after birth. Payment and binding advance promises subordinated the mother’s equal status before she could understand the bond. The center’s psychological warning that surrender might be difficult was neither disclosed nor pursued. Profit, financial inequality, and exploitation risks mattered even while the court acknowledged some satisfied surrogacy participants.

William’s right to procreate did not entail exclusive custody or extinguishment of another natural parent. The sperm-donor statute did not require identical treatment of a woman undergoing pregnancy and birth. State-law restoration made it unnecessary to decide Mary Beth’s separate constitutional companionship, state-action, or Thirteenth Amendment arguments. A hypothetical future statutory scheme’s constitutionality also remained open.

Comparisons with Kentucky’s different baby-selling interpretation, which still allowed withdrawal around birth, and Britain’s commercial-broker prohibition did not change New Jersey’s statutory protections. The court found no existing prohibition on voluntary unpaid arrangements permitting a change of mind and left reform to the legislature within constitutional limits.

sections.title: Custody turns on the child’s actual interests
sections.cue: Invalidity does not automatically return physical custody to Mary Beth
paragraphs: Between the natural parents, best interests controlled without an automatic sex preference. The court rejected using custody to punish illegal contracting and refused to imagine away the effects of the initial transfer order. Actual circumstances mattered even if judicial error contributed.

Credible expert evidence and the Stern home’s stability, nurturing, and openness supported William’s custody. The court criticized harsh judgments of Mary Beth’s understandable attachment and cautioned that money or education did not define an ideal life. It affirmed custody without finding either natural parent unfit. In future temporary disputes, an invalid contract alone would not justify removing a baby from the mother; highly persuasive evidence of danger, unfitness, or similar circumstances would be needed, with flight threats ordinarily addressed by an injunction.

sections.title: Legal motherhood is restored and visitation returns for decision
sections.cue: The remand does not reopen custody
paragraphs: Visitation had not been adequately litigated because termination made it unnecessary below. Mary Beth was entitled to visitation at some point, but form, conditions, and commencement required attention to both parents and the child’s paramount interests.

The unanimous seven-Justice court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded: William retained custody, Mary Beth’s parental rights were restored, and Elizabeth’s adoption was undone. A different judge would decide visitation through an abbreviated but reliable process within ninety days; appeal time was reduced to ten days with direct Supreme Court certification. This was a visitation remand, not a new custody determination or immediate unrestricted access order.
